title: Observability and Production Diagnosis
subtitle: Trace a slow or wrong answer to the hop that caused it, without turning telemetry into a second copy of customer data.
author: By Sourav Banerjee

practice_prompts.label: Discovery and the no-capture list
practice_prompts.hint: Split slow and wrong into measurable problems and name what telemetry may never hold.

practice_prompts.label: Both paths and the support workflow
practice_prompts.hint: Trace one request through the request path and the observability path, and how support reaches its hop.

practice_prompts.label: Failure policy and the dropped trace
practice_prompts.hint: Say which layers fail closed or degrade, and what you do when sampling lost the only bad trace.

practice_prompts.label: Incidents and rollout
practice_prompts.hint: Diagnose the latency and cost spikes from their spans, then name the rollout gates and owners.

rubric: Separates latency, correctness and diagnosability before proposing components.
Writes the no-capture list first and names a narrow, audited break-glass path.
Keeps the observability path unable to block, alter or authorise the request path.
Classifies and applies a keyed HMAC before storage, and treats a missing key as an error.
Biases sampling toward errors and slow traces, and runs the dropped-trace drill without treating a missing trace as health.
Fails closed on auth, cross-tenant lookup, redaction failure and audit evidence while letting export degrade.
Decomposes the latency incident by span against baselines and reads the cost incident's role_scope loss as a permission incident.
Gates rollout on trace coverage and telemetry overhead with named owners per phase.

editorial_review.evidence: Compared all 49 captured sections (dumped from source.json HTML with tables) against the rewrite item by item. The four overlapping tracks were folded into one path: the main guide's compact requirement and failure paragraphs were merged with the fuller Full Design tables in steps 3 and 6, the deep-dive incident bullets merged into the complete latency and cost spike dives, and the cheat-sheet kept as Quick review. Expansions are definitions the source assumed (span, trace, correlation ID, tenant, cardinality, exemplar, break-glass, cross-encoder, KV cache, prefill/decode), derived arithmetic that reproduces source figures (110-155 GB storage, 4x/9x queueing, 3.8 days of budget, ~20.2 s stage sum with a percentile caveat), and read-the-table paragraphs for both incident telemetry tables. Two additions are labelled as not from the source: the 0.95^3 sampling illustration and the 100%/90-day changed-constraint question. The Acme German refund trace became the brief's worked example; the external worksheet is disclosed as not imported. All seven figures in both variants are placed beside the text that walks them. November 20 complete maintained-baseline review: Complete maintained casebook: brief, eight walkthrough steps with all tables and figures, redaction, sampling, failure-drill, latency and cost incident, neighbouring-prompt and pivot deep dives, references, all practice answers and pivot cards, and Quick review. Targeted corrections and source-to-output mappings: /Users/sourav/Github_Repos/Forward-Deployed-Engineer-Interview-Prep/.website_spec/casebook-review-14-23-2026-11-20/observability-and-production-diagnosis/audit.json. Historical captured-source mappings remain preserved; this pass audits the maintained baseline. Source inconsistencies settled in text (2026-11-21): cost incident priced the GPT-4-class request at $2.74 (about 9× $0.31) while the 32K list prices give $1.44 for 21,384 in and 1,288 out → $1.44 and about 4.6× (also more consistent with a 3.8× bill on 7% more requests and contexts mostly over the 12,000-token routing threshold); a 12-second hard timeout beside a 22.18 s p95 → taught as limits at different boundaries (gateway timeout versus console measurement).
